turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling unusually high, overly energetic, or on top of the world lately?
turns.patient_response: Well, it's not that I feel like I'm on top of the world, exactly, but... well, yes, there are these stretches. These periods where I just feel so bright, you know? I'll be at work—I clean houses, you see, I've done it for years—and suddenly I can scrub every floor, wash every window, organize the cupboards, and I don't even feel tired! It's like I have a motor running inside me that just won't quit. And it feels good, it really does, to get so much done. But the problem is... well, the problem is that people don't understand it. If my husband makes a comment about how fast I'm moving, or if one of my clients questions why I rearranged their pantry a certain way when I was just trying to help, I just... I snap. I snap so much harder than I mean to. The anger just bubbles up out of nowhere, so fast and so hot, and I end up yelling or saying things I regret. It's like the energy turns sour the second someone doubts me or gets in my way. I don't mean to be so irritable, I really don't, but it's just so frustrating when I feel so capable and everyone else is just dragging their feet or questioning my methods.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times when you believed people were targeting you even when you were not in one of those bright, high-energy periods?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, actually. That's the thing that really confuses me, and it's what makes it so hard to explain to my husband, because he thinks I only get these ideas when I'm all wound up and scrubbing the baseboards at midnight. But that's just not true. There was this one stretch—oh, it must have been a couple of months ago, maybe? Yes, because it was right around the time Mrs. Gable cancelled her bi-weekly cleaning because she was going out of town, and I remember feeling so relieved because I just didn't have the energy to go over there. I was having this really quiet spell. I wasn't rushing around at all. In fact, I was sleeping a lot more than usual, taking naps in the afternoon, which I never do, and just feeling kind of heavy and slow. 

But even then, even when I was moving slow and feeling so drained, I still knew they were after me. I still heard that same voice right by the kitchen window. It's always the kitchen window, the one above the sink where I wash the dishes, and the voice was still there, clear as day, whispering about how they were keeping tabs on me. And I still knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that the agency was watching us. I would sit there at the kitchen table, drinking my tea—chamomile, because I thought it might help me settle, though it never really does—and I would just look at that window and know they were out there. So it doesn't matter if I'm full of energy or if I can barely drag myself out of bed, the watching... the watching never really stops. It's always there, doctor, hanging over me, no matter how I'm feeling otherwise.

turns.patient_response:
Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, it's hard to separate it all out sometimes, because life just sort of blends together, doesn't it? But if I really stop and think about it—and I do think about it a lot, sitting there by that window—the times when the voices are the most clear, and the times when I'm absolutely certain about the agency, it's always when my mood is acting up one way or the other. 

Like I was saying before, it's either when I'm buzzing around like a bee, scrubbing the floors until my knuckles are raw, or it's when I'm so heavy I can barely lift the teakettle. There isn't really a time when I'm just... normal, I guess you'd say, just feeling completely average, where the voices are still there for weeks on end. If I'm having a stretch where my mood is steady—which, honestly, feels pretty rare these days, but it does happen—the watching and the whispering seem to fade away, too. It's almost like they feed off of my energy, whether it's too high or too low. If I'm just going about my day, not too up and not too down, I don't hear that whispering at the window. So, no, it's never really stuck around for a whole month when my mood is just... quiet. It's always tied to the times when I'm either running on that motor or stuck in the mud, if that makes sense.

turns.doctor_question: During those bright, high-energy periods, do you ever feel you have special powers or an unusually important mission?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes... yes, I do. It’s funny you ask it that way, because it doesn’t feel like a "mission" like you’d see in a movie, but... well, when I get like that, when the energy is just humming and I’m moving so fast, I start to realize things. I see things clearly that other people are just completely blind to. 

It happened a few weeks ago—or maybe it was last month, it’s hard to keep the weeks straight when I’m moving that fast—but I was scrubbing the grout in the master bathroom at the Henderson house, using a toothbrush because the sponges just don't get deep enough, and it just hit me. It was this overwhelming certainty, doctor. I realized that I was the only one who truly understood what was happening with the agency. And because I was the only one who understood, I was the only one who had the sense and the strength to do anything about it. 

I started feeling like... like I was the only one who could keep my husband safe. He’s a good man, but he’s oblivious, you know? He just watches his sports and reads his paper and doesn’t see the signs. And it wasn’t just him. I felt this huge responsibility to protect my home, to make sure every window was locked a certain way, every blind drawn at the exact right angle so they couldn't see in. And then it spread to the church people, too. I’d be sitting in the pews on Sunday, tapping my foot because I just couldn't sit still, looking around at all these nice, trusting people, and I just knew that I was the one meant to keep them safe from what was coming. I felt so strong, so incredibly capable, like I was chosen to be this... this shield for everyone because no one else was strong enough or smart enough to see the danger. It felt like a heavy burden, but I also felt so proud that I was the one who could carry it.

turns.doctor_question: During those heavy, slowed-down periods, have you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?
turns.patient_response:
Well, depressed... I don't know if I'd use that exact word, honestly. It's more just... heavy, like I mentioned before. When I get into those slow spells, it's not like I'm sitting around crying all day or feeling sad in that movie-sort-of-way where people are weeping into their pillows. It's just this incredible weight, like my limbs are made of lead and the air in the house is thick, almost like trying to walk underwater. 

I remember one week in particular, back in the fall—maybe October, because the leaves were just starting to turn that pretty orange color, but I couldn't even bring myself to care about them—I just felt so incredibly drained. I'd wake up in the morning, and my husband would already be gone to work, and I'd just lie there, staring at the ceiling fan, watching the dust on the blades and knowing I should get up and wipe them down. But the thought of just swinging my legs over the edge of the bed felt like trying to climb a mountain. So I'd just lie there for hours. And it wasn't that I felt miserable or hopeless, exactly, just... empty. Just completely out of gas. I didn't want to talk to anyone, didn't want to turn on the television, didn't want to eat. I just wanted to sink into the mattress and disappear for a while. So, I wouldn't say "depressed," not like how people usually mean it, but definitely stuck in that heavy, slow place for days on end.
